newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals - Japan chrome prices seen unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals - Japan chrome prices seen unchanged.

text.p: Japanese users were expected to agree to fourth quarter prices for South African charge chrome at 42 cents a lb CIF, unchanged from the prior quarter and in line with Europe's fourth quarter negotiations, Japanese traders said on Tuesday.
They expected deals to be reached this week and next, while one said that some had already been concluded.

Another added, however, that individual arrangements may be made at lower prices, and traders said Japan's spot prices for high-carbon ferrochrome were hovering around 38 to 39 cents a lb for large orders.

They also noted talk that 10,000 tonnes of high-carbon ferrochrome were sold by a London trade house to a major Japanese steelmaker for October-December delivery at 37 cents a lb, although this was considered an unusual deal.

"I can't imagine anyone else doing that," said a ferrochrome trader for a large Japanese trade house, who added the seller appeared to be attempting to capture market share by offering attractive prices.
In the cobalt market, traders noted a slight easing of about $1 a lb in recent weeks, with western grade material quoted at $22 to $23 per lb CIF and Russian material at $21.
They said the Japan market was quiet, with users thought to hold sufficient stocks, but they expected prices would firm again in the weeks and months ahead.

"Consumption is slowly expanding in chemicals and aerospace," a European trader in Hong Kong said. "We will have to wait for other projects to come on line in Australia and Canada before we see movement in the price and that is two or three years away."
African producers' difficulties in meeting increased production targets and Russia's ongoing labour and power troubles were also cited as supportive factors for prices.
In Hong Kong and China, weak prices for antimony, indium and germanium dioxide were causing headaches for traders, who said some contracted deliveries from Chinese producers were not being honoured.

Chinese traders have garnered a reputation in past years for reneging on contracts if prices fell between order and delivery periods, and some Hong Kong traders said this was becoming more of a problem as prices headed downward.

A fall in the price of chemical products had contributed to a drop in the FOB (free on board) price of Chinese antimony to $2,050 to $2,100 a tonne, from $2,400 to $2,500 just a few weeks ago, a Chinese trading source said.
"Some producers and traders in China are saying they have 400 tonnes, 500 tonnes," he said.

Another trader said once the antimony price fell to $2,000 a tonne, Chinese sellers would not be interested. "We are getting close, and will be at $2,000 very soon," he said. "Some Chinese producers seem to be losing money already."
Prices for Chinese indium and germanium, used in making semiconductors, were also falling, Hong Kong traders said.
Indium was now going for $185 to $190 a kg, having plummeted from $400 a kg last month, a Chinese source said.

In Japan, Nippon Mining and Metals lowered its indium list price on Tuesday for the second time in less than one month to 26,000 yen per kg for large orders, a 4,000 yen decrease. The list price was at 59,000 yen per kilogram in February.
The Chinese source said germanium dioxide's drop had been nearly as dramatic to around $1,000 a kg from $1,400 in August, adding the problem was rising output, not a lack of demand.
Bismuth was also holding up well.
Chinese offers were starting at $3.30 to $3.50 a lb, one trader said, "which is high but we are able to negotiate that down (by) 10 to 20 cents".
"To Europe we are selling at $3.40 to $3.50 c&f, which is not too bad," he said.
-- Edmund Klamann, Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3 3432 6179), Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong News Desk (85-2 2843 6470)
